title: Effects of low sodium diet versus high sodium diet on blood pressure, renin, aldosterone, catecholamines, cholesterol, and triglyceride
authors: Graudal NA, Hubeck-Graudal T, Jurgens G
population: 195 randomised studies of low- versus high-sodium diets lasting 3 to 1100 days in people with normal or elevated blood pressure
funder: Internal sources: Copenhagen University Hospital Rigshospitalet (salary). External sources: the A.P. Møller Foundation for the Advancement of Medical Science, Denmark, a non-profit funding source that donated a grant for the pay of N. Graudal.
authorConflicts: None. All authors are employed at public institutions; none has any connection with or receives funds from the food and salt industries.
result: Sodium reduction from 203 to 65 mmol/day in white participants: systolic blood pressure -1.14 mm Hg (95% CI -1.65 to -0.63) with normal blood pressure (95 trials) and -5.71 mm Hg (-6.67 to -4.74) with hypertension (88 trials). During sodium reduction plasma renin activity rose by 1.56 ng/mL/h (1.39 to 1.73; 82 trials, 2904 participants), aldosterone by 104 pg/mL (88.4 to 119.7; 66 trials, 2506 participants), noradrenaline by 62.3 pg/mL (41.9 to 82.8), cholesterol by 5.19 mg/dL (2.1 to 8.3) and triglyceride by 7.10 mg/dL (3.1 to 11.1). The authors describe the hormone and lipid changes as potential side effects, more consistent than the blood-pressure effect.
